title: Who’s Responsible When AI Goes Wrong?
summary: When an AI incident reaches a regulator or a court, accountability lands on whoever can prove what happened. Here's what that takes at the data layer.
body_markdown:
### Summary


After an AI incident, the person who answers for it is whoever can produce the record of what happened. Accountability depends on evidence the data layer either keeps or doesn’t.


In 2024, a tribunal in British Columbia heard an argument that should worry anyone deploying AI at scale. Air Canada’s chatbot had told a grieving passenger he could apply for a bereavement fare after booking, which contradicted the airline’s actual policy. When he sued, Air Canada[argued the chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own statements](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2024-february/bc-tribunal-confirms-companies-remain-liable-information-provided-ai-chatbot/) . The tribunal rejected that, and the airline was found liable. The damages were only a few hundred dollars, but the verdict has much bigger implications for companies: You own what your AI does.


That settles the question of the company’s responsibility. But the question I get asked most often is the one underneath it: Inside the company, when an AI system leaks data, poisons a model, or produces a record that turns up in discovery, who’s responsible?


I get why people want a name. My honest answer is that the org chart won’t settle it; evidence will. **When an AI incident reaches a regulator, a judge, or your board, the person who ends up accountable is whoever can, or can’t, produce the record of what happened.** Everything else is a debate about titles.


## **The org chart hasn’t settled this, and the surveys say it won’t soon**


If you feel like AI governance landed on your desk without anyone deciding it should, you’re reading the situation correctly.


In[PwC’s latest “Global Digital Trust Insights” survey](https://www.pwc.com/us/en/services/consulting/cybersecurity-data-tech-risk/library/global-digital-trust-insights.html) of more than 3,900 leaders across 71 countries, less than 30% of organizations put AI accountability with their CIO, CTO, or another technology leader. About a quarter have a dedicated AI executive. Seventeen percent put it on the CISO. PwC’s own summary is that there isn’t yet one ownership model for AI governance and risk.


The security view of the same picture is sharper. Splunk’s[“The CISO Report](https://www.splunk.com/en_us/campaigns/ciso-report.html) ” found that 96% of CISOs now own AI governance and risk management, and 78% fear personal liability for a breach they’d have to answer for. Deloitte’s[technology leadership study](https://www.cybersecurity-insiders.com/ai-governance-ciso-authority-gap/) describes four roles that touch every AI agent an enterprise deploys: the CISO, the CTO, the CIO, and the chief data officer. Add the model vendor and the agent itself, and the line between who decided and who answers gets hard to find.


That’s a committee. Incidents don’t accept committee answers.


You might expect regulation to force the question. It’s doing the opposite. The EU just[pushed the AI Act’s high-risk obligations](https://www.gibsondunn.com/eu-ai-act-omnibus-agreement) from August 2026 to December 2027. Courts and regulators, meanwhile, haven’t waited.


The Air Canada tribunal needed no AI statute; it applied ordinary negligent-misrepresentation law to a chatbot. Privilege, consumer protection, securities disclosure, and negligence doctrine all predate[generative AI](https://www.everpuredata.com/knowledge/what-is-generative-ai.html) , and all of them apply to it today.


**Accountability for AI is arriving through existing law, and existing law doesn’t wait for your governance framework.**


## **The ‘something’ decides who’s on the hook**


“When something goes wrong” hides four different incidents, and each one lands on a different person:


- **An employee pastes sensitive material into a consumer AI tool.** The questions are what left, under what terms, and whether anyone approved that path. Whoever approved that path, or failed to define one, answers for it. In most companies, that’s the person who owns the approved AI paths for sensitive work, which means that if no one owns that list, this incident has no owner until the lawyers assign one.
- **A training set is**[poisoned or ingests compromised data](https://blog.everpuredata.com/perspectives/you-cant-build-trustworthy-agents-on-untrustworthy-data/) **upstream.** The model carries the compromise forward, and the fix is a rebuild from a clean copy. The person on the hook is whoever has to show which copy was clean and when. If no one can, the data platform owner inherits the problem by default.
- **An agent acts outside its scope.** An agent inherits the access of whatever identity it runs as. If that identity has no named human owner, the incident has no owner either, which is why the question “whose agent was this” should be answerable before the agent runs, as a matter of[workload identity](https://blog.everpuredata.com/purely-technical/beyond-guardrails-why-ai-infrastructure-security-is-hard/) rather than forensics.
- **An AI output turns up in discovery.** Prompts, outputs, and agent traces are corporate records. Whoever controls retention controls what exists to be produced, and what should have been disposed of defensibly and wasn’t.


Four incidents, four owners. But notice what the first question is in every case: Before anyone asks who’s at fault, they ask you to show them what happened.


## **Accountability is a records problem before it’s a people problem**


A regulator, an opposing counsel, or your own audit committee will ask some version of the same four things:


1. What data fed this system?
2. Who and what could reach it?
3. What did it actually do?
4. What did you know and when?


If the answers to those questions live in six tools and three vendors’ logs, nobody can assemble them in time, and the accountability conversation turns into the blame conversation.


So before deciding who owns an AI system, decide what the system must be able to prove. Four records, producible on demand:


- **Lineage and classification of what fed it.** Which data sets, which versions, what sensitivity. You can’t defend a model whose inputs you can’t describe, and the Everpure[“Global Data Sovereignty Report 2026](https://www.everpuredata.com/data-sovereignty/global-insights-report) ” found 62% of leaders lack full visibility into who can access, control, and manage their data. Start with[discovery and classification](https://www.everpuredata.com/products/data-intelligence.html) because that’s the record everything else depends on.
- **An access record that covers machines as well as people.** Human identities, workload identities, and agent identities, with the policy that applied at the time.
- **An immutable account of what the system did.** Agent traces and outputs that can’t be edited after the fact, retained under a policy you can state out loud.
- **A clean, time-stamped recovery copy.** Immutable snapshots on an[independent recovery path](https://blog.everpuredata.com/perspectives/never-mix-backup-and-production/) , with[anomaly detection](https://blog.everpuredata.com/solutions/from-anomaly-to-action-storage-intelligence-meets-cyber-recovery-2/) that tells you which copy to trust. A poisoned corpus is a recovery event, and the person who can produce a known-good copy is the person who gets to stop the retraining job instead of explaining it.


Every one of those is a property of the data layer, and that’s the point. **Governance at the data layer is what makes responsibility assignable because it’s what makes the evidence exist.**


A named owner without those records is a scapegoat with a title. A named owner with them can walk into the room and answer.


## **What I’d recommend doing next**


- **Name one accountable owner per AI system, and give them the records, not just the title.** A Northern Trust SVP put it plainly in a[recent interview](https://www.thedatawire.com/news/responsible-ai-governance-finance-kouassi-northern-trust) : You cannot tell the regulator the number changed because of AI. Someone signs. Make sure that person can see what they’re signing for.
- **Make “show me” a pre-approval requirement.** Before an AI system goes to production, ask whether the four records above can be produced within hours. If the answer is no, the system isn’t ready, whatever the model benchmarks say.
- **Treat every agent as an identity with a human owner.** Scope its access, log what it does, and know whose name is attached before the first task runs.
- **Put the AI estate under the same recovery and retention policy as everything else.** Training data, embeddings, and checkpoints are tier-one assets. They need immutable copies, tested restores, and retention rules that hold up in discovery.
- **Use tooling such as**[Solidcore.AI](http://solidcore.ai/) **to help actively monitor the AI surface area you’re trying to defend** , and put some policies in place to help identify and alert on anomalies. Automate governance early in the process.


“Who’s responsible” is usually asked looking for a name. The better version of the question is: When it happens, who can prove what happened? Build so the answer is “we can,” and the name on the org chart matters a great deal less.


---


## **FAQs**


### **Who is responsible for AI governance in an enterprise?**


There is no settled model. Recent surveys show accountability split across CIOs, CTOs, CISOs, chief data officers, and dedicated AI executives, with the CISO increasingly holding it by default. In practice, the person who answers for an incident is whoever can produce the records of what the system ingested, who could access it, and what it did.


### **Who is liable when an AI system causes a data breach or a bad outcome?**


Existing law applies before AI-specific regulation does. Courts and regulators look at who controlled the data, who approved the tool, and what records exist, and they have already held companies responsible for what their AI tools say and do. The organization is liable to its customers and regulators; inside the organization, liability follows whoever owned the decision and the evidence.


### **Should the CISO own AI governance?**


The CISO is often the nearest risk-aware leader, which is why most now hold it, but AI governance spans legal, procurement, data, and business decisions a CISO doesn’t control. A workable model names one accountable owner per AI system and gives that owner the data layer records needed to defend decisions.


### **What records should an organization keep for its AI systems?**


Lineage and classification of training and inference data, an access record covering human and machine identities, an immutable log of outputs and agent actions under a stated retention policy, and a clean, time-stamped recovery copy of training data and checkpoints.
